titulo: Walking in, and being served without apologising
subtitulo: Greet on the way in, ask for what you want, and stop hedging — the Spanish bar rewards all three
permissao: You are allowed to take up space. Order directly, speak louder than feels polite, and drop the padding — 'ponme una caña, por favor' is not rude, it is the normal register at a Spanish bar, and the five layers of 'would you mind' are what leave you unserved.
espelho: The run-up you put in front of a request at home — sorry, I was just wondering, if it's not too much trouble — is the bit that reads as odd there. It lands as distance, not as manners, and the barman serves the person behind you.
frasePiso: You will walk into a Spanish bar, greet the room, order in four words and sign off on the way out. Most people who spend a fortnight in Spain never once greet a room they walk into.

fichasCulturais.sinal: You walk into a small shop with four people in it and somebody says 'buenos días' to the air; on the way out, a cashier you will never see again says 'hasta luego'.
fichasCulturais.suaLeitura: Greeting a room full of strangers is over-familiar, and saying see-you-later to someone I will never see again is a lie. Better to keep quiet and not intrude.
fichasCulturais.oQueEAli: The greeting is what opens the counter. Walking in silently is not neutral there — it reads as slightly rude, and the service you get quietly reflects it (docs/pesquisa-espanha.md §7.2, regra 1).
fichasCulturais.oQueVoceFaz: Say 'buenos días' to the air on the way in — shop, bar, bakery, waiting room and the lift — and 'hasta luego' on the way out. If you cannot work out which one, 'buenas' always lands.
fichasCulturais.oQueMelhora: You stop being the silent foreigner at the end of the counter and start being served like everybody else, for the price of one word.
fichasCulturais.ondeNaoVale: Not in a big supermarket, on the metro or in a hotel breakfast room. The greeting is for a room with a counter and somebody behind it, not for every space that happens to have strangers in it.

fichasCulturais.sinal: A twenty-five-year-old barman calls you 'tú' from the first word, and if you answer with 'usted' he may laugh and tell you not to make him feel old.
fichasCulturais.suaLeitura: Formal is the safe option with a stranger. If I use the polite form I cannot possibly cause offence.
fichasCulturais.oQueEAli: Spain tuteia far more than Latin America does — in bars, shops, restaurants and taxis 'tú' is the default, and 'usted' with somebody your own age creates distance instead of respect (RAE/ASALE, Nueva gramática básica §10.6.2; docs/pesquisa-espanha.md §4.1).
fichasCulturais.oQueVoceFaz: Uniform, white coat or grey hair — usted. Everything else — tú. And if they tú you, tú them straight back.
fichasCulturais.oQueMelhora: You sound like somebody who has been here before instead of somebody reading from a manual, and the counter warms up in one turn.
fichasCulturais.ondeNaoVale: Not with the police, the Guardia Civil or a public official — that is the one place where informality causes real friction — and not with somebody clearly elderly until they invite you. Andalusia ustedea a little more freely, and there usted costs you nothing.

fichasCulturais.sinal: You order at the volume you think is polite, the barman moves on to somebody else, and the room around you is a great deal louder than you are.
fichasCulturais.suaLeitura: They ignored me. Either they would rather not serve a foreigner, or my Spanish came out wrong.
fichasCulturais.oQueEAli: The room is loud, and the volume that reads as polite at home does not carry across a bar. He did not ignore you — he did not hear you.
fichasCulturais.oQueVoceFaz: Speak up, louder than feels comfortable, with eye contact and a slightly raised hand and 'perdone'. Never click your fingers, never wave money.
fichasCulturais.oQueMelhora: You get served inside the two seconds the barman is looking at you, instead of going home believing you were snubbed.
fichasCulturais.ondeNaoVale: Not in a small restaurant dining room, at a hotel breakfast counter or in a pharmacy. There the room is quiet and the same volume lands as shouting.

fatosDatados.afirmacao: Spain is a tú country: tú is the default in bars, shops, restaurants and taxis, and usted is for three places — police and officials, somebody clearly elderly, and a formal counter.
fatosDatados.fonte: RAE/ASALE, Nueva gramática básica §10.6.2 «tú y usted»; Moreno Fernández (CVC); Aleza cap. 4 — sintetizados em docs/pesquisa-espanha.md §4.1

fatosDatados.afirmacao: 'Buenos días' runs until lunch, and lunch there is about two in the afternoon; after that it is 'buenas tardes', until it goes dark.
fatosDatados.fonte: docs/pesquisa-espanha.md §5.A (fichas 2 e 3) e a tabela de horários de refeição — la comida 14:00–15:30/16:00

steps.pt: Part 1B. Quick warm-up before we start, because under pressure your English mouth comes straight back: hand on the leg, one tap per syllable, all the same size. Say it with me — mu-chas gra-cias. Four taps. Flat palm on the vowels, nothing slides. Right. Today is the smallest, highest-value skill in the whole course: walking into a place and being served. That sounds trivial. It is not. There is a version of you that stands quietly at a Spanish bar for twenty minutes being invisible, and a version that has a beer in ninety seconds, and the difference between them is about six words and one social habit that will feel rude to you and isn't.

Habit first, because it costs nothing and buys a lot. In Spain you greet the room on the way in. Shop, bar, bakery, waiting room, and yes — the lift. You walk into a small shop with four people in it and you say 'buenos días' to the air, and the air says it back. Walk in silently and you haven't been neutral, you've been slightly rude, and the service you get will quietly reflect that. Same on the way out: 'hasta luego', even to a cashier you will never see again in your life. 'Buenos días' runs until lunch — and Spanish lunch is two in the afternoon, so it's a longer morning than yours. After that it's 'buenas tardes'. And if you can't work out which, there's a wildcard that always works and sounds very local: 'buenas'.
Hi, good morning. — The H is silent. Five flat vowels, no sliding.

steps.promptPt: It's nine in the morning and you're pushing open the door of a tiny bakery. Two customers turn round to look at you. Greet the room. Speak now.
steps.pt: Hi, good morning.
Good afternoon. — From about two in the afternoon until it goes dark. The switch is lunch, not midday.

steps.promptPt: It's four in the afternoon and you're walking into a pharmacy for sun cream. The pharmacist looks up. Greet her. Speak now.
steps.pt: Good afternoon.

Guiri alert, and this one is aimed squarely at the British. Here is how we order a beer at home: 'Sorry, hi, sorry — I was just wondering, if it's not too much trouble, whether I could possibly get a beer? If that's alright? Whenever you get a chance, no rush at all.' Say the Spanish translation of that at a busy bar in Madrid and one of two things happens. Either the barman loses the thread halfway through and serves the bloke behind you, or he decides you are being oddly formal and cools right down. What Spanish people actually say is four words: 'ponme una caña, por favor.' Put me a small beer, please. To an English ear that lands like an order barked at a servant. It isn't. It's normal, and it's friendly. The politeness in Spanish lives in your tone and in one 'por favor' at the end — not in five layers of 'would you mind'. Drop the padding. You will get served faster and liked more.
A small draught beer, please. — 'Una caña' is the national unit: a small glass of draught. Ask for 'a beer' and you'll get an expensive bottle.

steps.promptPt: Busy bar, three deep, and the barman has just looked straight at you. You have about two seconds. Order a small draught beer — no apology, no hedge. Speak now.
steps.pt: A small draught beer, please.

Now, that 'ponme' is the informal 'you' — tú. And here I have to correct something you have probably been taught. If you learned any Spanish at school in the States, or from an app, you learned to be formal with strangers because formal is safe. In Spain that is upside down. Spain is a tú country. Bars, shops, restaurants, taxis, anyone roughly your age or younger — tú. Fire off 'usted' at a twenty-five-year-old barman and you won't offend him, but you will create distance and mark yourself as someone reading from a manual; you may even get teased for it. Save 'usted' for exactly three places: police and officials, someone clearly elderly, and a formal counter — a bank, a hospital, a smart hotel. The pocket version: uniform, white coat or grey hair, use usted. Everything else, tú. And if they tú you, tú them straight back.

steps.es: Perdone, ¿me pone un café con leche, por favor?
steps.pinyin: pehr-DOH-neh, meh POH-neh oon kah-FEH kohn LEH-cheh, por fah-BOR
steps.pt: Excuse me, could I have a white coffee, please? — The usted version. Note the endings: perdonE, ponE. The tú version is perdonA, ponES.
steps.tts: Perdone, ¿me pone un café con leche, por favor?

steps.promptPt: You're at the counter of a very proper old café and the waiter is about seventy, in a white jacket. This is an usted moment. Get his attention and ask for a white coffee. Speak now.
steps.es: Perdone, ¿me pone un café con leche, por favor?
steps.pinyin: pehr-DOH-neh, meh POH-neh oon kah-FEH kohn LEH-cheh, por fah-BOR
steps.pt: Excuse me, could I have a white coffee, please?

Two words to say and two words to recognise. To say: 'perdona' — or 'perdone' — is how you get someone's attention, anyone, anywhere: the waiter, a stranger in the street, the person blocking the aisle. 'Perdón' on its own is for bumping into someone. 'Lo siento' is a real apology, for real damage, and English speakers massively overuse it — don't say 'lo siento' to summon a waiter, it's like saying 'I'm so terribly sorry' when you want the bill. And the two to recognise: when it's your turn at the bar, the barman will fire something at you. It'll be 'dime' — literally 'tell me' — or '¿quién va?', who's next. That is not a difficult question. It is your cue. Answer it, out loud, immediately. Look him in the eye. If you look at the floor and wait politely for your turn, you will still be waiting in twenty minutes.
👂 'Who's next? Go ahead.' — You never have to say this. You absolutely have to recognise it, because it means the window is open and it closes fast.

Last piece: getting out of there. 'Vale' is the most Spanish word in existence — it's 'ok', 'right', 'got it', 'fine', and you will hear it roughly four hundred times a day. Say it, it costs nothing and it fits everywhere. 'Gracias' you have. If someone thanks you, the answer is 'de nada'. And then 'hasta luego' on the way out — see you later — which in Spain is said sincerely to people you will demonstrably never see later. A permission before we finish, and it matters for the British in particular: the bar is loud. Spanish bars are loud. If you speak at the volume you think is polite, you will not be heard, and you'll go home believing Spanish waiters ignored you. They didn't hear you. Speak up — louder than feels comfortable. That's the normal volume, not an argument.
OK, thanks. See you later. — The whole exit, in five words.

steps.promptPt: You've paid, you've got your bread under your arm and you're heading for the door. Sign off on the way out — yes, even though you'll never see her again. Speak now.
steps.pt: OK, thanks. See you later.
Say it with him. Short, level, no apology in front of it.

Bar manners in focus. Four things, then you're free. One: 'por favor' and 'gracias' once per interaction, at the end — not on every single turn. Spanish uses far fewer of them than English does, and stacking them up sounds ceremonious rather than warm. Two: no small talk with the cashier. 'Hola' going in, 'hasta luego' going out, and nothing in between is required. Three: never click your fingers, never wave money, never shout 'chico'. Eye contact and a slightly raised hand with 'perdone' is the whole technique. And four, the permission I'd most like you to actually use: you are allowed to take up space. Order directly. Speak up. Sit at a bar with one drink for an hour if you like — nobody is going to move you on, that's an Anglo habit and it doesn't exist here.

Part 1B done. You can walk in, greet the room, get a barman's attention, order without a paragraph of apology in front of it, choose between tú and usted without panicking, and leave properly. Next up, part 1C: the repair kit — what you say when the answer comes back at full speed and you understand nothing at all. Which will happen, on day one, and is completely fine. See you there.
The wildcard greeting. Works any time of day, sounds local, costs one word.

aprofundar.titulo: Greetings, tú and usted, in writing (optional)

secoes.corpo: 'Buenos días' runs from waking up until lunch — and Spanish lunch is 14:00, so it covers far more of the day than 'good morning' does. 'Buenas tardes' runs from lunch until dark. 'Buenas noches' covers both arriving late and leaving. 'Hola' is neutral and works at any hour. 'Buenas' on its own is the informal wildcard: it sounds very local, it never lands wrong, and it costs you nothing. '¿Qué tal?' is a light 'how's it going' — it is not a request for a medical report, and the expected answer is 'bien, ¿y tú?' or just a nod.

exemplos.pt: BWEH-nahs NOH-chehs — good evening / goodnight, arriving or leaving

secoes.titulo: The four pairs: tú and usted, side by side
secoes.corpo: You do not need to learn Spanish conjugation. You need four phrases in two versions each, and that covers essentially every counter you will ever stand at. The pattern to notice: the tú form usually ends in -s or -a, the usted form in -e.

Getting this wrong in a bar costs you nothing but a bit of distance. There is exactly one situation where informality causes real friction: police, Guardia Civil and public officials. Use usted there without exception. Also default to usted with someone clearly elderly whom you don't know, until they invite you to do otherwise — and they often will, sometimes with a joke about how usted makes them feel old. At a doctor's, a bank or a smart hotel it is genuinely neutral either way. Regional note: the south tends to use usted a little more freely than the north, so if you are in Andalusia and in doubt, usted costs you nothing.

secoes.titulo: Six body rules for a Spanish bar
secoes.corpo: 1. Greet on the way in, sign off on the way out — shops, bars, waiting rooms and lifts. 2. Order short and loud; the hedge makes the barman lose the thread. 3. Volume is higher than you think is polite, and it is not aggression. 4. The bill never comes on its own — bringing it unasked is treated as throwing you out, so you must ask: 'la cuenta, por favor', or mime writing in the air. 5. Waiters don't come back to check how everything is tasting; you summon them with eye contact and 'perdone'. 6. Never snap your fingers, never wave a note, and know that the table is yours after you've paid — nobody is going to hurry you out.
